Compatibility with lme4, glmmTMB, brms and INLA

Source: vignettes/articles/compatibility.Rmd
compatibility.Rmd

Four packages shaped how a mixed or latent Gaussian model is written and fitted in R. lme4 (Bates et al. 2015) introduced the (1 + x | g) formula syntax for random effects and fits generalized linear mixed models by maximum likelihood, with a Laplace or adaptive Gauss-Hermite approximation to the integral over each group. glmmTMB keeps that syntax, computes the Laplace approximation with automatic differentiation through TMB, and adds families such as the negative binomial and Tweedie, zero-inflation through ziformula, and restricted (REML) estimation for non-Gaussian responses. brms translates the same formulas into a Stan program and samples the full posterior with the No-U-Turn sampler, with priors set per parameter class. INLA (Rue, Martino and Chopin 2009) computes posterior marginals for latent Gaussian models by nested Laplace approximations, writes each structured effect as an f() term, and supplies the penalised-complexity (PC) priors and the scaled BYM2 areal model that tulpa uses as its defaults.

tulpa takes the lme4 formula syntax and the INLA latent blocks into one Bayesian engine. Blocks that a deterministic approximation handles well are fitted by Laplace or nested Laplace, as in INLA, and the directions where that approximation is biased can be corrected by exact sampling, as in Stan. The fit records which method ran. This article checks that, with matched model, settings and priors, tulpa gives the same estimates as each of the four packages, and documents the places where it does not. Each comparison runs on one simulated data set, so it shows agreement of the numbers on that data set and says nothing about calibration over repeated data, which the Simulation-based calibration article covers.

Installation is covered in Get started. The comparisons need lme4, glmmTMB and brms from CRAN, and INLA, which is not on CRAN; its DESCRIPTION names the repository https://inlabru-org.r-universe.dev. Every chunk that calls another package runs only when that package is installed. The brms fit uses cmdstanr as its Stan backend when CmdStan is set up, and rstan otherwise.

library(tulpa)

How agreement is measured

A comparison is only meaningful when both packages fit the same model to the same data and report the same quantity. Each section below states three things before its fits: the model, the estimand (maximum likelihood, restricted likelihood or a posterior summary) and, for the Bayesian fits, the priors on every parameter. Where one of these cannot be matched, the section says so and the table shows the gap that follows.

Agreement is reported per parameter as the difference between the tulpa estimate and the other package’s, in the parameter’s units and in units of the other package’s standard error or posterior SD. A difference of 0.01 SD is numerical noise; a difference of 0.5 SD changes what a reader would conclude. The helper below builds that table from two named vectors of estimates and two of standard errors.

agree <- function(est_t, se_t, est_o, se_o) {
  data.frame(tulpa = est_t, tulpa_se = se_t, other = est_o, other_se = se_o,
             diff = est_t - est_o, diff_in_se = (est_t - est_o) / se_o)
}

To check agreement on your own data, fit the model in both packages with the settings of the matching section, pass the estimates and standard errors to agree(), and read the last column.

Random-intercept GLMM: tulpa, lme4 and glmmTMB

A binary response measured in 40 groups of 8 is the setting where the Laplace approximation to a group’s integral is least accurate, so it is a demanding first test. The intercept is -0.4, the slope 0.9, and the group intercepts are drawn with SD 0.8.

G <- 40L; npg <- 8L
g <- rep(seq_len(G), each = npg)
x <- rnorm(G * npg)
u <- rnorm(G, sd = 0.8)
y <- rbinom(G * npg, 1, plogis(-0.4 + 0.9 * x + u[g]))
d <- data.frame(y = y, x = x, g = factor(g))

lme4 and glmmTMB maximise the Laplace-approximated likelihood over the fixed effects and the random-intercept SD. The tulpa backend that does the same is mode = "agq": with n_quad = 1 its marginal is the same joint Laplace approximation, and tol tightens the optimiser (the default tolerance is discussed under Differences).

tm <- list()
tm$tulpa_agq <- system.time(
  f_t <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "binomial", mode = "agq",
               control = list(n_quad = 1L, tol = 1e-10))
)[["elapsed"]]
summary(f_t)$coefficients[, 1:2]
#>               estimate std.error
#> (Intercept) -0.4873948 0.1864441
#> x            0.9396841 0.1568559
f_t$sigma_re
#> [1] 0.8160032
tm$glmer <- system.time(
  f_l <- lme4::glmer(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = binomial)
)[["elapsed"]]
tm$glmmTMB <- system.time(
  f_g <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = binomial)
)[["elapsed"]]
c(logLik_tulpa = f_t$log_marginal, logLik_glmer = as.numeric(logLik(f_l)),
  logLik_glmmTMB = as.numeric(logLik(f_g)))
#>   logLik_tulpa   logLik_glmer logLik_glmmTMB 
#>      -186.8587      -186.8594      -186.8587

tulpa and glmmTMB reach the same log-likelihood to four decimals, and glmer’s default optimiser stops 0.0007 below it. The table therefore compares the estimates against glmmTMB. The random-intercept SD has no standard error in either package’s default output, so its last two columns are empty.

se_g <- sqrt(diag(vcov(f_g)$cond))
tab_ml <- agree(
  c(coef(f_t), sigma = f_t$sigma_re),
  c(summary(f_t)$coefficients[, "std.error"], NA),
  c(glmmTMB::fixef(f_g)$cond, sigma = sqrt(glmmTMB::VarCorr(f_g)$cond$g[1])),
  c(se_g, NA))
round(tab_ml, 5)
#>                tulpa tulpa_se    other other_se diff diff_in_se
#> (Intercept) -0.48739  0.18644 -0.48740  0.18645    0      0e+00
#> x            0.93968  0.15686  0.93968  0.15686    0     -1e-05
#> sigma        0.81600       NA  0.81600       NA    0         NA

The same match holds for adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature. lme4 calls the number of nodes nAGQ; tulpa calls it n_quad. With seven nodes the integral over each group of eight binary responses is no longer a Laplace approximation, and the SD estimate moves from 0.816 to 0.842 in both packages.

f_t7 <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "binomial", mode = "agq",
              control = list(n_quad = 7L, tol = 1e-10))
f_l7 <- lme4::glmer(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = binomial, nAGQ = 7)
rbind(tulpa = c(coef(f_t7), sigma = f_t7$sigma_re),
      glmer = c(lme4::fixef(f_l7), sigma = attr(lme4::VarCorr(f_l7)$g, "stddev")))
#>       (Intercept)         x     sigma
#> tulpa  -0.4891310 0.9406283 0.8418408
#> glmer  -0.4891226 0.9406310 0.8418574

Random slopes: tulpa and glmmTMB

A random slope adds a covariance matrix: the intercept SD, the slope SD and their correlation. lme4 fits it for this Poisson response as well, but glmmTMB also offers the restricted likelihood, which is the estimand of tulpa’s empirical-Bayes backend. Simulate 60 groups of 12 counts with SDs 0.7 and 0.5 and correlation 0.4.

G2 <- 60L; npg2 <- 12L
g2 <- rep(seq_len(G2), each = npg2)
x2 <- rnorm(G2 * npg2)
Sig <- matrix(c(0.49, 0.14, 0.14, 0.25), 2)
b2 <- t(t(chol(Sig)) %*% matrix(rnorm(2 * G2), 2))
y2 <- rpois(G2 * npg2, exp(0.2 + 0.5 * x2 + b2[g2, 1] + b2[g2, 2] * x2))
d2 <- data.frame(y = y2, x = x2, g = factor(g2))

mode = "eb" maximises the Laplace marginal over the covariance with the fixed effects integrated out, which is the restricted (REML-type) estimate. hyperprior = "flat" removes the default PC and LKJ prior on the covariance, so nothing but the likelihood enters the maximisation; the fixed effects keep the default normal(0, 2.5) prior, which is weak against 720 observations. The glmmTMB call is the same formula with REML = TRUE.

tm$tulpa_eb <- system.time(
  s_t <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 + x | g), data = d2, family = "poisson",
               mode = "eb", hyperprior = "flat")
)[["elapsed"]]
tm$glmmTMB_reml <- system.time(
  s_g <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 + x | g), data = d2, family = poisson,
                          REML = TRUE)
)[["elapsed"]]
vc <- glmmTMB::VarCorr(s_g)$cond$g
tab_rs <- agree(
  c(coef(s_t), sd_int = s_t$map$sigma[1], sd_x = s_t$map$sigma[2],
    cor = s_t$map$rho),
  c(summary(s_t)$coefficients[, "std.error"], NA, NA, NA),
  c(glmmTMB::fixef(s_g)$cond, attr(vc, "stddev"),
    cor = attr(vc, "correlation")[1, 2]),
  c(sqrt(diag(vcov(s_g)$cond)), NA, NA, NA))
round(tab_rs, 5)
#>               tulpa tulpa_se   other other_se     diff diff_in_se
#> (Intercept) 0.36146  0.09205 0.36216  0.09268 -0.00070   -0.00752
#> x           0.37336  0.08274 0.37397  0.08370 -0.00061   -0.00734
#> sd_int      0.66035       NA 0.66030       NA  0.00005         NA
#> sd_x        0.57221       NA 0.57218       NA  0.00003         NA
#> cor         0.56860       NA 0.56850       NA  0.00010         NA

The SDs and the correlation agree to 1e-4, and the fixed effects differ by under a hundredth of a standard error.

The Bayesian counterpart integrates over the covariance instead of fixing it at the maximum. With mode = "laplace" a slope term routes to that integration (the Random slopes article covers it). The posterior medians of the two SDs equal the restricted estimates to two decimals, and the median of the correlation is 0.52 against the restricted 0.57, inside an interval from 0.25 to 0.73.

s_n <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 + x | g), data = d2, family = "poisson",
             mode = "laplace", control = list(n_threads = 2))
summary(s_n)$hyperparameters[1:3, c("parameter", "median", "ci_lo", "ci_hi")]
#>   parameter    median     ci_lo     ci_hi
#> 1   sigma_1 0.6618372 0.5385379 0.8241984
#> 2   sigma_2 0.5730461 0.4599580 0.7214724
#> 3    rho_12 0.5227020 0.2459051 0.7251218

Areal BYM2 model: tulpa and INLA

The BYM2 model splits a region’s effect into a scaled ICAR part and an independent part, with a total SD sigma and a mixing weight for the structured share. INLA calls the weight phi and parameterises the scale as a precision; tulpa calls the weight rho and reports sigma directly. Both scale the ICAR part so that its marginal variances have geometric mean one (Riebler et al. 2016), which spatial_bym2() does and INLA’s scale.model = TRUE does.

Simulate Poisson counts on a 10 by 10 lattice of regions with rook adjacency, expected counts between 10 and 60, a slope of 0.4 and a field with total SD 0.6, 70% of its variance spatially structured.

nr <- 10L; K <- nr * nr
W <- matrix(0, K, K)
id <- function(i, j) (i - 1L) * nr + j
for (i in 1:nr) for (j in 1:nr) {
  if (i < nr) W[id(i, j), id(i + 1L, j)] <- W[id(i + 1L, j), id(i, j)] <- 1
  if (j < nr) W[id(i, j), id(i, j + 1L)] <- W[id(i, j + 1L), id(i, j)] <- 1
}
cx <- rep(1:nr, each = nr); cy <- rep(1:nr, nr)
s  <- as.numeric(scale(sin(cx / 3) + cos(cy / 3)))
bf <- 0.6 * (sqrt(0.7) * s + sqrt(0.3) * rnorm(K))
x3 <- rnorm(K); E <- round(runif(K, 10, 60))
y3 <- rpois(K, E * exp(-0.3 + 0.4 * x3 + bf))
d3 <- data.frame(y = y3, x = x3, E = E, region = factor(1:K), id = 1:K)

Matching the priors

The priors have to be set on the INLA side to match tulpa’s defaults, since the two packages’ defaults differ.

Parameter tulpa default INLA default INLA setting used here
total SD sigma PC prior, P(sigma > 3) = 0.01 pc.prec, P(sigma > 1) = 0.01 pc.prec with param = c(3, 0.01)
mixing weight uniform on (0, 1) pc, P(phi < 0.5) = 2/3 logitbeta with param = c(1, 1) (uniform)
intercept normal(0, 2.5) flat flat
slope the same normal, precision 0.001 normal, precision 0.001

INLA’s pc.prec with param = c(U, alpha) states P(1 / sqrt(precision) > U) = alpha, which is the same statement as tulpa’s PC prior on sigma. The fixed-effect priors are left at each package’s default, normal(0, 2.5) in tulpa against a flat intercept and a precision of 0.001 in INLA; the conditional check below measures how much that matters here.

tm$tulpa_bym2 <- system.time(
  a_t <- tulpa(y ~ x + offset(log(E)) + spatial(region), data = d3,
               family = "poisson",
               spatial = spatial_bym2(W, level = "group", group_var = "region"),
               mode = "nested_laplace", control = list(n_threads = 2))
)[["elapsed"]]
#> [nested-laplace] preparing joint Hessian sparsity pattern
#> [nested-laplace] 1/30 cells (3%) | elapsed 0s | ETA >=0s | 0.00s/cells
#> [nested-laplace] 7/7 cells (100%) | elapsed 0s | ETA done | 0.00s/cells
#> [nested-laplace] preparing joint Hessian sparsity pattern
#> [nested-laplace] 1/25 cells (4%) | elapsed 0s | ETA >=0s | 0.00s/cells
#> [nested-laplace] 22/22 cells (100%) | elapsed 0s | ETA done | 0.00s/cells
summary(a_t)$hyperparameters[, c("parameter", "mean", "sd")]
#>   parameter      mean         sd
#> 1     sigma 0.5149011 0.04965631
#> 2       rho 0.7223863 0.13517381
hyp <- list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(3, 0.01)),
            phi  = list(prior = "logitbeta", param = c(1, 1)))
tm$inla_bym2 <- system.time(
  a_i <- INLA::inla(
    y ~ x + f(id, model = "bym2", graph = W, scale.model = TRUE,
              constr = TRUE, hyper = hyp),
    family = "poisson", E = E, data = d3, num.threads = "2:1",
    control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0, prec = 0.001))
)[["elapsed"]]
sd_marg <- INLA::inla.tmarginal(function(t) 1 / sqrt(t),
                                a_i$marginals.hyperpar[[1]])
sd_inla <- unlist(INLA::inla.zmarginal(sd_marg, silent = TRUE)[1:2])
hp <- summary(a_t)$hyperparameters
tab_bym2 <- agree(
  c(coef(a_t), sigma = hp$mean[1], mixing = hp$mean[2]),
  c(summary(a_t)$coefficients[, "std.error"], hp$sd),
  c(a_i$summary.fixed$mean, sd_inla[["mean"]], a_i$summary.hyperpar$mean[2]),
  c(a_i$summary.fixed$sd, sd_inla[["sd"]], a_i$summary.hyperpar$sd[2]))
round(tab_bym2, 4)
#>               tulpa tulpa_se   other other_se    diff diff_in_se
#> (Intercept) -0.2244   0.0354 -0.2425   0.0360  0.0181     0.5025
#> x            0.4416   0.0571  0.4468   0.0572 -0.0052    -0.0906
#> sigma        0.5149   0.0497  0.5083   0.0495  0.0066     0.1326
#> mixing       0.7224   0.1352  0.7083   0.1251  0.0141     0.1125

The slope and the total SD agree to within 0.2 posterior SD, and the mixing weight’s mean differs by 0.014, and tulpa’s posterior SD for it is 0.14 against INLA’s 0.13. The intercept differs by half a posterior SD, and the next section traces that gap to the method rather than the model.

The same model at fixed hyperparameters

Fixing sigma and the mixing weight removes the outer integration, so the two packages then solve the same inner problem: the posterior of the fixed effects and the field given the hyperparameters. In tulpa that is one cell of the nested-Laplace grid. prior_from_spec() turns the spatial_bym2() spec into the prior list that tulpa_nested_laplace() reads, and the grid is set to the single cell sigma = 1 / sqrt(5), mixing weight 0.8.

pr <- prior_from_spec(spatial_bym2(W, level = "group", group_var = "region"),
                      d3)
pr$sigma_grid <- 1 / sqrt(5); pr$rho_grid <- 0.8
c_t <- tulpa_nested_laplace(d3$y, rep(1L, K), cbind(1, d3$x), prior = pr,
                            family = "poisson", offset = log(d3$E),
                            control = list(n_threads = 2, axis_refine = "none"))
#> [nested-laplace] preparing joint Hessian sparsity pattern
#> [nested-laplace] 1/1 cells (100%) | elapsed 0s | ETA done | 0.00s/cells
#> [nested-laplace] 1/1 cells (100%) | elapsed 0s | ETA done | 0.00s/cells
eta_t <- as.numeric(c_t$fitted_eta[1, ]) - log(d3$E)
c_t$modes[1, 1:2]
#> [1] -0.2155708  0.4366814

On the INLA side the precision is fixed at 5 and phi at 0.8. INLA reports the posterior mean of the linear predictor; by default that mean includes a variational-Bayes correction, which is switched off here and kept on below.

hyp_fix <- list(prec = list(initial = log(5), fixed = TRUE),
                phi  = list(initial = qlogis(0.8), fixed = TRUE))
cond_inla <- function(vb) INLA::inla(
  y ~ x + f(id, model = "bym2", graph = W, scale.model = TRUE,
            constr = TRUE, hyper = hyp_fix),
  family = "poisson", E = E, data = d3, num.threads = "2:1",
  control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0, prec = 0.001),
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
  control.inla = list(control.vb = list(enable = vb)))
c_i0 <- cond_inla(FALSE); c_i1 <- cond_inla(TRUE)
rbind(vb_off = c(c_i0$summary.fixed$mean,
                 max_abs_eta_diff = max(abs(eta_t - c_i0$summary.linear.predictor$mean))),
      vb_on  = c(c_i1$summary.fixed$mean,
                 max_abs_eta_diff = max(abs(eta_t - c_i1$summary.linear.predictor$mean))))
#>                             max_abs_eta_diff
#> vb_off -0.2155973 0.4368528     0.0001490837
#> vb_on  -0.2316248 0.4405133     0.0439807996

With the correction off, INLA’s fixed effects equal tulpa’s to within 2e-4 and the linear predictors of the 100 regions agree to within 2e-4, so the two packages build the same model, the same scaling and the same constraint, and the fixed-effect priors make no visible difference. With the correction on, the intercept moves by 0.016, close to the 0.018 gap of the full fits above. tulpa’s inner solve reports the Laplace mode; INLA’s default reports a mean corrected towards the skew of the Poisson posterior. The Differences section shows the full fit with the correction switched off.

A brms fit of the GLMM

brms samples the posterior of the random-intercept model from the first section. The matched tulpa fit integrates the random-intercept SD over a grid with adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature inside each group (control$re_cov = "aghq"), under the same priors:

  • the fixed effects, intercept included, normal(0, 2.5) in both;
  • the SD, tulpa’s PC prior P(sigma > 3) = 0.01, which for a random-effect SD is an exponential with rate -log(0.01) / 3, written out for brms.

brms writes the intercept as an ordinary coefficient (0 + Intercept) so that the normal(0, 2.5) prior applies to it on the same scale as in tulpa. The sampler runs two chains of 1000 iterations, half of them warmup.

rate <- -log(0.01) / 3
pri <- c(brms::set_prior("normal(0, 2.5)", class = "b"),
         brms::set_prior(sprintf("exponential(%.6f)", rate), class = "sd"))
tm_brms <- system.time(
  f_b <- brms::brm(y ~ 0 + Intercept + x + (1 | g), data = d,
                   family = brms::bernoulli(), prior = pri, chains = 2,
                   iter = 1000, warmup = 500, cores = 2, seed = 1, refresh = 0,
                   backend = if (has_cmdstan) "cmdstanr" else "rstan")
)[["elapsed"]]
tm$tulpa_aghq <- system.time(
  f_q <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "binomial",
               mode = "structured",
               control = list(re_cov = "aghq", n_threads = 2))
)[["elapsed"]]
fb <- brms::fixef(f_b)
#> Loading required namespace: rstan
sb <- brms::VarCorr(f_b)$g$sd
hq <- summary(f_q)$hyperparameters
tab_brms <- agree(
  c(coef(f_q), sigma = hq$mean[1]),
  c(summary(f_q)$coefficients[, "std.error"], hq$sd[1]),
  c(fb[, "Estimate"], sb[, "Estimate"]),
  c(fb[, "Est.Error"], sb[, "Est.Error"]))
round(tab_brms, 4)
#>               tulpa tulpa_se   other other_se    diff diff_in_se
#> (Intercept) -0.4853   0.1910 -0.4992   0.1888  0.0138     0.0732
#> x            0.9350   0.1562  0.9419   0.1724 -0.0069    -0.0398
#> sigma        0.8308   0.2302  0.8387   0.2370 -0.0079    -0.0334

The posterior means of the fixed effects agree to within 0.08 posterior SD and the mean of the SD to within 0.04. The brms posterior SDs of the slope and of the random-intercept SD are 0.016 and 0.007 larger than tulpa’s. The effective sample sizes of the brms draws set the Monte Carlo error of its means:

fx <- summary(f_b)$fixed
cbind(fx[, c("Est.Error", "Bulk_ESS")],
      mcse_in_sd = 1 / sqrt(fx[, "Bulk_ESS"]))
#>           Est.Error  Bulk_ESS mcse_in_sd
#> Intercept 0.1887669  987.2551 0.03182624
#> x         0.1724471 1488.0502 0.02592336

A brms mean carries a Monte Carlo error of about 0.03 posterior SD here, so the difference in the slope’s mean is 1.5 Monte Carlo standard errors and the difference in the intercept’s 2.3.

Measured agreement

The table collects the largest difference, in units of the other package’s standard error or posterior SD, over the parameters of each comparison that carry one.

worst <- function(tab) max(abs(tab$diff_in_se), na.rm = TRUE)
data.frame(
  comparison = c("binomial GLMM, ML (glmmTMB)", "Poisson random slope, REML",
                 "Poisson BYM2 (INLA, defaults matched)", "binomial GLMM (brms)"),
  max_abs_diff_in_se = round(c(worst(tab_ml), worst(tab_rs),
                               worst(tab_bym2), worst(tab_brms)), 3))
#>                              comparison max_abs_diff_in_se
#> 1           binomial GLMM, ML (glmmTMB)              0.000
#> 2            Poisson random slope, REML              0.008
#> 3 Poisson BYM2 (INLA, defaults matched)              0.502
#> 4                  binomial GLMM (brms)              0.073

Syntax map

The tables give the tulpa equivalent of each formula term, family, structured effect, prior and accessor of the four packages. Every tulpa function named here is exported by tulpa 0.7.8.

Formula terms and data

lme4 / glmmTMB / brms INLA tulpa
(1 | g) f(g, model = "iid") (1 | g)
(1 + x | g) f(..., model = "iidkd") (1 + x | g)
(1 + x || g) f(g, model = "iid") plus f(g2, x, model = "iid") (1 + x || g)
(1 | a/b), (1 | a) + (1 | b) one f() per term the same
offset(log(E)) E = E (Poisson) or offset() offset(log(E))
cbind(s, n - s) ~ ... (lme4), s | trials(n) (brms) Ntrials = n s ~ ... with n_trials = n
weights = w weights = w weights = w
ziformula = ~ 1 (glmmTMB) zeroinflatedpoisson1 family ziformula = ~ 1
dispformula = ~ x (glmmTMB) no equivalent
nAGQ = 7 (lme4) mode = "agq", control = list(n_quad = 7)
REML = TRUE (glmmTMB) mode = "eb", hyperprior = "flat"

Families

glmmTMB / lme4 brms INLA tulpa family =
binomial bernoulli(), binomial() "binomial" "binomial"
poisson poisson() "poisson" "poisson"
nbinom2 negbinomial() "nbinomial" "neg_binomial_2"
nbinom1 "neg_binomial_1"
truncated_poisson, truncated_nbinom2 "truncated_poisson", "truncated_neg_binomial_2"
gaussian gaussian() "gaussian" "gaussian"
lognormal lognormal() "lognormal" "lognormal"
Gamma Gamma() "gamma" "gamma"

tweedie "tweedie" "tweedie" (power in phi2)

family_names() lists the tulpa families. tulpa holds a family’s dispersion fixed at phi unless estimate_phi = TRUE under mode = "eb"; the other packages estimate it by default.

f(id, model = "bym2", graph = W) spatial(region) with spatial = spatial_bym2(W, level = "group", group_var = "region")

f(t, model = "rw1", replicate = g) temporal = temporal_rw1("t", group_var = "g")

f(id, model = "generic0", Cmatrix = Q) latent(tgmrf(...))

Differences

The differences below are design choices of tulpa, each with the code in both packages. They follow from two decisions: every scale tulpa does not integrate or estimate is an argument the call states, and a fit reports the inference method that produced it.

A random-intercept SD is conditioned on under mode = "laplace"

lme4 and glmmTMB estimate the random-intercept SD in every fit. In tulpa, mode = "laplace" on a random-intercept model conditions on sigma_re, the value the call supplies, and warns when none is supplied. The default mode = "auto" and mode = "structured" integrate the SD instead, and mode = "agq" and mode = "eb" estimate it.

f_c <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "binomial",
             mode = "laplace", sigma_re = 0.8)
coef(f_c)
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>  -0.4515672   0.8755364
VarCorr(f_c)
#>   term        coef  sd      source
#> 1    g (Intercept) 0.8 conditioned

The source column reads conditioned, so the fit carries the SD it was given. The estimated SD of the same model is in the ML table of the first section.

Empirical-Bayes variances are restricted estimates

mode = "eb" integrates the fixed effects out of the marginal likelihood before maximising over the variances, so with hyperprior = "flat" it gives the restricted estimate of glmmTMB’s REML = TRUE, here to within 0.002. It does not reproduce the maximum-likelihood fit of lme4 and of glmmTMB’s default, whose SD is smaller.

f_e <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "binomial", mode = "eb",
             hyperprior = "flat")
f_r <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = binomial,
                        REML = TRUE)
c(tulpa_eb = f_e$map$sigma, glmmTMB_reml = sqrt(glmmTMB::VarCorr(f_r)$cond$g[1]),
  ml = f_t$sigma_re)
#>     tulpa_eb glmmTMB_reml           ml 
#>    0.8423350    0.8440785    0.8160032

A dispersion is estimated only on request

glmmTMB estimates the negative-binomial size along with everything else. tulpa holds it at phi by default; estimate_phi = TRUE under mode = "eb" estimates it, again as a restricted estimate.

y_nb <- rnbinom(G * npg, mu = exp(1 + 0.5 * x + u[g]), size = 2)
d_nb <- data.frame(y = y_nb, x = x, g = factor(g))
f_nb <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d_nb, family = "neg_binomial_2",
              mode = "eb", hyperprior = "flat", estimate_phi = TRUE, phi = 1)
g_nb <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d_nb,
                         family = glmmTMB::nbinom2, REML = TRUE)
c(tulpa_size = f_nb$phi, glmmTMB_size = glmmTMB::sigma(g_nb))
#>   tulpa_size glmmTMB_size 
#>     2.809925     2.809590

INLA’s default mean correction

INLA applies a variational-Bayes correction to the posterior mean of the latent field by default, which the conditional check above isolated. tulpa’s nested Laplace reports the mixture of the per-cell Laplace modes. Switching INLA’s correction off brings the full fit to tulpa’s numbers.

a_i0 <- INLA::inla(
  y ~ x + f(id, model = "bym2", graph = W, scale.model = TRUE,
            constr = TRUE, hyper = hyp),
  family = "poisson", E = E, data = d3, num.threads = "2:1",
  control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0, prec = 0.001),
  control.inla = list(control.vb = list(enable = FALSE)))
rbind(tulpa = coef(a_t), inla_vb_on = a_i$summary.fixed$mean,
      inla_vb_off = a_i0$summary.fixed$mean)
#>             (Intercept)         x
#> tulpa        -0.2244064 0.4416127
#> inla_vb_on   -0.2424737 0.4467936
#> inla_vb_off  -0.2244228 0.4423572

The two choices answer different questions about a skewed posterior: INLA’s corrected mean moves the estimate towards the posterior mean, tulpa keeps the Laplace centre and leaves the skew to its diagnostics and to an exact sampler.

Incomplete rows are refused

lme4, glmmTMB and brms drop a row with a missing value under their default na.action; INLA treats a missing response as a value to predict. tulpa refuses a missing predictor, so the rows a fit uses are always the rows supplied. A missing response is read as INLA reads it on tulpa’s nested-Laplace path, which leaves the row’s likelihood term out and still forms its linear predictor; every other backend refuses it.

d_na <- d; d_na$x[3] <- NA
tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d_na, family = "binomial", mode = "agq")
#> Error:
#> ! Non-finite value(s) in the model matrix (1 row(s), first at row 3). tulpa does not drop incomplete cases; remove or impute NA/NaN/Inf in the predictors before fitting.
nobs(lme4::glmer(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d_na, family = binomial))
#> [1] 319

Optimiser tolerance of the AGQ backend

At its default tolerance, mode = "agq" reaches the same maximum on this data set: the log-likelihood and the SD equal those of the tol = 1e-10 fit to the printed digits, and the SD differs from glmmTMB’s by 1e-7. The fits above set tol = 1e-10.

f_d <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "binomial", mode = "agq",
             control = list(n_quad = 1L))
rbind(default_tol = c(logLik = f_d$log_marginal, sigma = f_d$sigma_re),
      tol_1e_10   = c(f_t$log_marginal, f_t$sigma_re),
      glmmTMB     = c(as.numeric(logLik(f_g)),
                      sqrt(glmmTMB::VarCorr(f_g)$cond$g[1])))
#>                logLik     sigma
#> default_tol -186.8587 0.8160032
#> tol_1e_10   -186.8587 0.8160032
#> glmmTMB     -186.8587 0.8160033

Timings

The timings are elapsed seconds of one run of each fit above, measured on a shared Windows 11 workstation (beast) with R 4.6.1, two threads where a fitter takes them, with tulpa 0.7.8. The data sizes are 320 binary responses in 40 groups (GLMM), 720 counts in 60 groups (random slope) and 100 regions (BYM2). One run of a fit under a second carries noise of the order of its own value, so the table shows the order of magnitude and not a ranking; it says nothing about how the packages scale to larger data.

tm$brms <- tm_brms
data.frame(fit = names(tm), seconds = round(unlist(tm), 2), row.names = NULL)
#>            fit seconds
#> 1    tulpa_agq    0.14
#> 2        glmer    0.11
#> 3      glmmTMB    0.08
#> 4     tulpa_eb    0.13
#> 5 glmmTMB_reml    0.11
#> 6   tulpa_bym2    0.31
#> 7    inla_bym2    1.76
#> 8   tulpa_aghq   10.98
#> 9         brms   49.78

The three maximum-likelihood fits of the random-intercept model take the same time to the precision of one run. The BYM2 fit took 0.31 seconds in tulpa and 1.76 seconds in INLA. The brms time includes compiling the Stan model, which a cached model skips on the next run, and the tulpa AGQ integration of the same model spends its time on nine-node quadrature inside each group at every grid cell.

When the other package is the better choice

  • lme4 for linear mixed models fitted by REML with lmer(), and for profile likelihood intervals on the variance components.
  • glmmTMB when the dispersion itself depends on covariates (dispformula), or the zero-inflation part carries random effects.
  • brms for distributional and non-linear models, any likelihood Stan can write, and exact sampling of the whole posterior with Stan’s diagnostics.
  • INLA for its wide range of likelihoods and f() models, per-region BYM2 summaries read directly from summary.random, and the inlabru interface for spatial point processes.

All four have years of use and published validation behind them. tulpa’s agreement rests on its own test suite and on comparisons such as the ones in this article.

References

Bates, D., Maechler, M., Bolker, B. and Walker, S. (2015). Fitting linear mixed-effects models using lme4. Journal of Statistical Software 67(1), 1-48. doi:10.18637/jss.v067.i01

Riebler, A., Sorbye, S. H., Simpson, D. and Rue, H. (2016). An intuitive Bayesian spatial model for disease mapping that accounts for scaling. Statistical Methods in Medical Research 25(4), 1145-1165.

Rue, H., Martino, S. and Chopin, N. (2009). Approximate Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models by using integrated nested Laplace approximations. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 71(2), 319-392.
